content.thinking:
Drafting the postmortem now, I want to flag some key nuances: the error rate stayed flat, so this was purely a latency issue, not an error spike. More importantly, the recovery timing shows metrics improved at 07:27, before the scale-out actually took effect at 07:27:56 — so attributing the fix to the scale-out may be a false assumption I should call out. I also haven't determined whether the traffic surge was organic or a retry storm.

I'll avoid restating the given impact figures as if I computed them, describing impact qualitatively instead while still citing the traffic rise and CPU limit as supporting evidence. For the executive summary, I'll avoid specific component names and use generic descriptions instead, then keep the root cause section to just a sentence or two before listing out my assumptions.

assumptions: The metrics place recovery at 07:27, which is before the scale-out was applied at 07:27:56. The service returning to baseline is therefore not demonstrably a result of the scale-out; the traffic surge may simply have subsided on its own. The mitigation was marked CONFIRMED on the basis of a healthy check at 07:29:09, which does not distinguish between the two.

The traffic surge is assumed to be organic demand. The investigation explicitly noted it could equally be a client-side retry storm or other non-organic driver, and that no signal in the evidence (no deploys in the prior ~31 hours, no feature-flag changes, no dependency slowdown) separates the two. This alternative was never tested.
CPU saturation is inferred to be the binding constraint from cpu_used_cores pinning at the 3.0-core limit; no thread-pool, connection-pool, or downstream-dependency saturation was ruled out directly.
The ClientDisconnected log entries are assumed to be shopper abandonment caused by latency rather than a distinct client-side fault.

Only the service's own metrics, logs, and change events were examined. Whether upstream or neighbouring services were also affected by the same traffic was not checked, so the blast radius is assumed to be limited to this service's account pages.
input.executive_summary: Between 07:13 and 07:27 UTC on 28 September 2026, the account pages of the online shop became slow to load. Traffic to the service rose to roughly four times its normal level and the service did not have enough compute capacity to keep up, so pages took far longer than usual to render. Shoppers who gave up and closed the page before it finished loading show up in the logs as failed requests, but the proportion of requests that failed did not rise above its normal level during the incident — the harm here was waiting, not outright errors. Automated monitoring alerted at 07:27, investigated, and added more capacity to the service; the service was measured back at its normal performance shortly afterwards and the incident was closed as mitigated. A draft code change has been opened for engineers to review. The underlying reason for the traffic surge has not yet been identified.
input.root_cause: Request volume to io-shop rose roughly four-fold (about 1,200 to 5,400 req/min) starting around 07:08Z against a fixed CPU allocation of 3.0 cores across 3 replicas; CPU usage tracked the traffic and pinned at the limit from 07:16Z, so requests queued and p50/p95/p99 latency blew out. The ClientDisconnected errors in the logs are shoppers abandoning slow account pages — a symptom of the saturation, not its cause. Why traffic quadrupled was not established.
